questions.:question/problem: Which of the following shows some of the solution curves of the differential equation $x\cdot\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1$ for $x>0$?
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Rearranging the equation, we get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}$.

Integrating the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =1\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =1\ln|x|+C \\ y & =\ln{\left(x \right)}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plot the solution curves by selecting different values for $C.$ The sketch below shows the solution curves for $C=-2,0,2$ for $x>0$.

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?

{{field-1}}$=1$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=9$ and the vertical radius has length $b=2.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{9}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{81}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
